The Board

Everything Comes Due in December

A four-point declaration signed by three presidents in Shenzhen, and the dated decisions that follow it: a European summit on November 26, the Federal Reserve on December 9, and the Texas grid audit on December 10.

Scroll

Shenzhen

The room was the prize.

Xi Jinping hosted the first meeting of an American president with the leaders of Russia and China together, in the city China built to prove its model. The text the three men signed fits on an index card.

Photograph by Charlie fong, via Wikimedia Commons. The Futian district of Shenzhen, the Ping An Finance Centre at the centre, across Xiangmi Lake. Shenzhen was a fishing county before it became China’s first Special Economic Zone in 1980.

What’s Moved

Three presidents met in Shenzhen on November 19 and signed a four-point declaration that names no war, sets no date, and caps nothing. What it does not contain is the story.

Ukraine hit the Crimean Bridge for the third time in a week on the morning of the summit.

In Berlin the same day, Ukraine’s European backers met with the two American envoys who carry the negotiation. No guarantee was signed. The money Europe is offering for 2027 is still a proposal that all 27 member states must approve.

The Federal Reserve’s October minutes, released November 18, say almost every official on the committee expects another rate increase. Markets price a quarter-point hike on December 9 as close to certain, and the live argument is now about a half point.

In Texas, the environmental regulator resumed reviewing data center permits on November 13, before the grid audit that was supposed to gate them is finished.

Verdict

The Shenzhen declaration is four points of agreement among three governments that agree on almost nothing else, and its only clause with a specific target is the one shielding sitting officials from the International Criminal Court. That clause pays one man in the room. The rest of the text commits nobody to anything, and everyone in the room knew it before they sat down: a senior American official said in advance that no agreement was expected and Ukraine was not on the agenda.

What moved this week moved elsewhere, on dates that are already fixed. Europe’s veto over any Ukraine settlement is money and troops, and both are still unapproved and unmanned. The Federal Reserve decides on December 9. The Texas grid audit reports on December 10. The board is not being set in summit rooms this month. It is being set by calendars.

Chapter One

The Room in Shenzhen

Xi hosted, Trump was the guest who mattered most, and Putin left with the one clause in the text that pays a specific man: the one shielding sitting officials from the International Criminal Court.

Xi Jinping greeted Donald Trump on the tarmac in Shenzhen with a red carpet, honor guards and a fighter jet flyover. Vladimir Putin was greeted by a Politburo Standing Committee member. The order of the greetings was the first honest document of the week: China hosts, America is the guest who matters most, Russia is in the room but not at the head of it.

Shenzhen was chosen to argue something. The city was a fishing county before it became China’s first Special Economic Zone in 1980, a test ground for market policies. Hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit there, China’s third time hosting after Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014, puts that experiment on display. The 21 APEC economies came to talk about trade, technology and supply chains.

The part they remember is the meeting on November 19, the first time an American president has sat at a dedicated negotiating table with the leaders of Russia and China together. It lasted between about 60 and 90 minutes by the conflicting press accounts, including opening remarks to cameras. Before it, Trump met Putin alone for about 42 minutes and Xi for about an hour.

The text they produced fits on an index card. The three countries, as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, committed to reform the UN so it can respond more effectively. They plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products, and they reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows. They recognized that state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials are paramount, and agreed the International Criminal Court and similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction. And they reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought, and said they will hold a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation.

Read it for what is missing. Ukraine is not in it. Iran is not in it. There is no warhead number, no cap, no inspection, no date for the dialogue, and no follow-up meeting announced.

The nuclear sentence deserves a closer look, because it sounds like progress and is a quotation. The line about a nuclear war never being winnable comes from the joint statement Ronald Reagan and Mikhail Gorbachev issued at Geneva in 1985. All five nuclear weapon states repeated it together in January 2022. What has changed since is subtraction: the New START treaty, the last agreement capping American and Russian strategic arsenals at 1,550 deployed warheads, expired on February 5, 2026. For the first time in more than 50 years there is no legally binding limit and no inspection regime. A dialogue about reducing risks, with no numbers attached, is what three governments say when the treaty is gone and none of them will name a replacement.

China has already named its price for staying out. Beijing has said repeatedly that it is neither fair, reasonable nor realistic to ask China to join nuclear negotiations at this stage, when its arsenal, estimated by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute at about 620 warheads in January, is a fraction of the American and Russian stockpiles of more than 5,000 each. Shenzhen did not move that position by a word.

The trade clock did not move either. The American and Chinese tariff truce, extended in November, holds the added American tariff on Chinese goods at 10 percent and suspends the rest until January 10, 2027. That date, not anything said in Shenzhen, is the next real event in the relationship. China closed the first ten months of 2026 with a trade surplus of $1.04 trillion, including $266.5 billion with the United States. A surplus that size is why Washington needs the truce and why Beijing can afford to host a summit that produces four points.

So who gained? Xi gained the room. The format was his stage, in his showcase city, and he was not pulled into either war. Putin gained the photograph and the court clause. He arrived as the only leader in the room under an International Criminal Court arrest warrant, issued in 2023, and left with the United States and China signed onto language that the court must not abuse its jurisdiction. That is the one concrete transfer of the day, and it cost the other two nothing they value. Trump gained a picture of great-power management with no commitment attached, which is also what he paid with: the format itself, three men deciding in a room the affected countries were not in.

Putin said there was nothing wrong with Yalta, the 1945 meeting where America, Britain and the Soviet Union divided the postwar order. The comparison fails on the facts, and the failure is instructive. Yalta ran eight days, the three were wartime allies, and they allocated territory their armies already occupied. Shenzhen ran under two hours, the three are rivals in unfinished wars, and they allocated nothing. Chancellor Friedrich Merz, speaking after the Berlin meeting, called Shenzhen above all a photo opportunity and said a Yalta format will not bring peace to Europe. Exclusion creates a counter-coalition, and the counter-coalition met the same day, 5,000 miles west.

Chapter Two

The War Underneath

While the presidents posed, Ukraine hit the Crimean Bridge for the third time in a week, the front did not move, and Russia aimed its air war at winter heat.

While the presidents were posing in Shenzhen, the war they did not name was not waiting for them.

Early on Thursday, November 19, Ukraine struck the Crimean Bridge for the third time in a week. The bridge, 19 kilometers long and opened in 2018, is Russia’s fixed link to Crimea and a main supply route for its forces in the south. Monday’s attack did minor damage. Tuesday’s destroyed the central road section: a span of the main road arch collapsed into the Kerch Strait, in video verified by Reuters. Thursday’s attack halted rail traffic, Russian authorities said, and some trains were running again by the afternoon. Nobody was reported hurt in the third strike, and its damage is still unassessed. The bridge is damaged and partly closed. It is not destroyed.

The operation behind the strikes is the larger fact. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine used drone versions of its Palianytsia cruise missile against the road section, and Neptune, Ruta and FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles against the railway section. The Institute for the Study of War, a Washington research group that maps the war daily, describes it as the seventh stage of a campaign run over several weeks, which first suppressed the air defenses, radars and electronic warfare systems around the bridge. A Ukrainian officer told The Times the final strikes were flown without SpaceX’s satellite network, using drones as radio relays instead. A weapon that no longer needs an American satellite link is a weapon no American decision can switch off. That matters for every negotiation that assumes Washington can simply turn Ukraine’s strike capability down.

On the ground, the front did not move. The Institute for the Study of War recorded no advance by either side on November 17 and none on November 18. In its October accounting, Russian forces seized about 140 square kilometers and lost about 167, a net loss of about 27 square kilometers in the month they were supposed to be grinding forward. The heaviest fighting stays where it has been: the Pokrovsk direction, around Dobropillia, and at Kostiantynivka, the town that shields the Kramatorsk and Sloviansk line. Since the start of October, 80 percent of Russian attacks on Ukraine’s fortress belt of prepared defensive positions in Donetsk have fallen on those two axes.

The fighting on those axes has names and formations. Toward Kostiantynivka, Russia’s 8th Combined Arms Army is running infiltration missions into the town itself: small groups slip into its northern and central streets, and Ukrainian infantry and drone operators holding positions inside the town strike them there, in footage geolocated on November 17 and 18. Farther west, Russia’s 51st Combined Arms Army is tasked with encircling the fortress belt from near Dobropillia and Pokrovsk. A Russian milblogger claimed on November 18 that its forces had seized Rohanske, a village about 10 kilometers beyond the closest assessed Russian position. The claim is the advance. The army is not there.

Attrition is running against the attacker. Janis Kluge, an economist at a German research institute, counted about 263,000 contracts signed in the first nine months of 2026 from Russian Finance Ministry data, roughly 1,000 recruits a day. Ukrainian General Staff figures, carried by the Institute for the Study of War, put Russian casualties at an average of about 2,270 a day so far in November, after the highest monthly losses of the war in October. Casualty claims in this war are contested and Kyiv’s are the source here, so treat the exact numbers with care. The direction is corroborated by the recruiting arithmetic: an army taking in about 1,000 men a day cannot sustain losses at twice that rate without either slowing down or reaching for men it has so far avoided calling up.

The air war runs the other way, and it is aimed at winter. Russia launched 141 long-range drones, 73 of them jet-powered, on the night of November 17 to 18 alone. Ukraine’s Energy Ministry says Russia has struck energy facilities more than 1,000 times since September, most of them the high-voltage substations that move power from power stations to cities. The British government, announcing aid in Berlin, put its own count of attacks on energy infrastructure above 2,000, a wider category stated without a start date, and said daily outages have reached 16 hours in several regions and up to 22 hours in Kyiv. The United Nations human rights office reported 372 Ukrainian civilians killed and 1,981 injured in October, a 95 percent increase on October 2025, with long-range strikes causing 55 percent of the casualties. Heat, not territory, is Russia’s winter lever: a population kept cold is pressure on Kyiv that no declaration in Shenzhen mentions.

Ukraine’s answer is to burn Russia’s fuel system. On the night of November 17 to 18, Ukrainian strikes hit the Ilsky and Afipsky refineries in Krasnodar Krai, in southern Russia. Reuters reported on November 18, citing two industry sources, that Russian crude processing has fallen about 45 percent from more than 700,000 tonnes a day in late October to about 400,000 tonnes a day, with 15 of Russia’s 35 major refineries disrupted or halted. The same reporting carries the limit: the November average is still above 500,000 tonnes a day, only 5 to 10 percent below September and October. The run rate is a crisis for Russian motorists and military diesel supply. The monthly average is not yet a collapse. The gap between the run rate and the monthly average is the difference between a campaign that is working and one that has worked.

Ukraine’s General Staff counted 211 combat clashes in the day to November 19, with 71 Russian airstrikes and about 4,600 kamikaze drones. Those are Kyiv’s figures, published by the side doing the counting, and they measure intensity rather than outcome. The outcome measure is the map, and it shows two armies spending men and drones to hold the same ground.

Chapter Three

Berlin Holds the Veto

Europe cannot be settled over, because only Europe can supply the guarantee force and the 2027 money. Both are still unapproved, and the money decision lands on November 26 and 27.

The Berlin meeting was not improvised in response to Shenzhen. Europe named its negotiating team six days earlier, in Dublin on November 13: the European Union institutions plus France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the United Kingdom. On November 19 those leaders, with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte and President Zelenskyy, met at the Chancellery under Chancellor Merz. More than 30 governments were represented in the wider Coalition of the Willing gathering. German officials said the focus was robust and legally binding security guarantees that would come into force after a ceasefire.

The American envoys were inside that room, not outside it. Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner came to Berlin to brief the allies on Trump’s talks in China and to work on guarantees, an economic recovery plan, and the shape of the next negotiating round. That is a reporting line from Shenzhen to Berlin. It is not the same as an American commitment, and no American commitment was published.

Moscow, meanwhile, is contesting whether Europe belongs in the talks at all. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov said on November 17 that there is no talk of European participation in future negotiations. The Institute for the Study of War notes that this directly contradicts what Witkoff and Kushner have argued for. So the format fight has three live positions, not a settled exclusion: Russia says Europe is out, the American envoys say Europe is in, and Europe is paying to make its seat real.

Europe’s seat is real for a specific reason. A ceasefire line that nobody will guarantee is a pause, not a settlement, and only European states can supply the force that makes a guarantee physical. That force is 2,800 soldiers from 11 countries, led by France and Britain, and it is exercising now for the first time: training in Poland, in Romanian airspace and in the western Black Sea from November 9 to 22. The honest limits matter as much as the fact. The force trains with light equipment and no tanks, it deploys only after a ceasefire, the United States is not part of it, and NATO was informed rather than involved. It is a promise being rehearsed, not an army in the field.

The European Union’s existing support loan for Ukraine is 90 billion euros for 2026 and 2027. Money is moving under it: a payment of 1.71 billion euros on November 16 brought what Ukraine has received under the loan’s defense component to 18.1 billion euros, with 23.6 billion euros still available for the rest of 2026.

The gap is 2027. The European Commission estimates Ukraine will need about 70 billion euros more that year, and on November 18 it proposed a new loan of up to 45 billion euros, up to 25 billion for military support and 20 billion for budget support, borrowed on capital markets against the European Union budget. Ukraine would repay the principal only if Russia pays reparations. The proposal needs approval from all 27 member states. An extraordinary European summit on November 26 and 27 is where the financing options land next.

Behind the proposal sits the asset Europe has not used. About 210 billion euros of Russian central bank assets are frozen in the European Union, most of them held at Euroclear, the securities depository in Belgium. Of roughly 8 billion euros in windfall profits generated on the assets, 3.8 billion euros has been delivered to Ukraine so far. Euroclear’s chief executive warned on November 13 that transferring the assets without their matching liabilities would bankrupt the depository, and demanded permanent guarantees from European states. Belgium carries the legal risk if Russia sues or retaliates, while the benefit is shared by 27 countries. Until the other 26 indemnify the one, the largest single pool of money in this war stays a headline rather than a flow.

Britain’s contribution in Berlin shows how pledges work at the national level. Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced a 260 million pound package built around more than 1,000 long-range strike drones, some able to fly more than 1,000 kilometers, plus maritime, logistics and surveillance drones. More than 80 percent of the money will be spent in the United Kingdom. No drone models and no delivery dates were published. It follows a separate 240 million pound air defense package announced on November 17, with more than 1,000 short-range missiles and deliveries from mid-December. The first package is industrial policy and signaling as much as firepower, and it should be read that way. The second has dates attached.

Shenzhen’s three presidents cannot deliver a post-ceasefire force, European-scale financing, or relief from European sanctions. Berlin can withhold all three. A veto holder meeting on the same day as a summit is not the weaker event, even when the veto holder has not yet written the check its veto depends on.

Chapter Four

The Price of Money

The week's most consequential document was the Federal Reserve's October minutes: almost every official expects another increase, and the committee's own members named the data center boom as an inflation risk.

The most consequential document of the week was not signed in Shenzhen or Berlin. It was published in Washington at 2 in the afternoon on November 18: the minutes of the Federal Reserve’s October 27 and 28 meeting.

The Federal Reserve, America’s central bank, sets the federal funds rate, the overnight interest rate banks charge each other, which anchors borrowing costs across the economy. Its rate-setting committee is the Federal Open Market Committee. A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so a 25 basis point move is a quarter of a point. The current rate range is 3.75 to 4.00 percent, after an increase in September and a hold in October.

The October hold was not comfortable. The vote was 10 to 2, and both dissenters, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, wanted an increase at that meeting. The minutes say almost all participants judged that further increases would likely be appropriate, and a couple of them said a move of more than 25 basis points could deserve consideration in December if the inflation data were unfavorable. Many participants also named the artificial intelligence building boom itself as a material source of inflation risk, a central bank saying that the data center race is pushing up the price of money that the data center race borrows. Remember that sentence when this report reaches Texas.

The data since October have not rescued the doves, the officials who favor lower rates. October’s jobs report, released November 6, added 165,000 jobs, and revisions added another 84,000 to August and September combined, taking the three-month average to about 137,000 a month. The unemployment rate was 4.1 percent. Inflation is stuck: consumer prices rose 0.4 percent in October, and core prices, which strip out food and energy to show the underlying trend, rose 0.3 percent for the third straight month. There is no October inflation rate for the year as a whole, because the government did not collect October 2025 prices during the 2025 funding lapse, so no 12-month comparison exists. The last complete annual readings are September’s. On the Fed’s own preferred gauge, the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, which measures prices across everything households consume including costs paid on their behalf, prices rose 3.6 percent in the year to September, and core PCE, the same index without food and energy, rose 3.1 percent. The Fed’s target is 2 percent. October’s PCE figures arrive November 25.

Weekly jobless claims, the fastest signal of layoffs because they are counted weekly and barely revised, show a labor market that is cooling at the edges rather than cracking. In the week ending November 14, 203,000 people filed a first claim, while 1.76 million were still claiming for the week ending November 7, up 70,000 in a week. Firing is historically low. Hiring is slowing. That combination gives the Fed room to raise rates and a reason to watch December 4, when November’s jobs report lands, five days before it votes. November’s inflation report lands December 10, one day after the vote. The Fed will decide the price of money without seeing the newest inflation number. That is not a criticism. It is the calendar, and it is why the argument inside the committee is about January as much as December.

Governor Christopher Waller has made himself the argument. On November 10 he said he leaned toward a quarter-point increase in December, and that if October core inflation ran at 0.3 percent or higher, as it had in August and September, a half-point increase should be considered. It ran at exactly 0.3 percent. On November 18, before the minutes were published, Waller went further: either the Fed raises by a half point in December, or it signals clearly that another increase follows in January. New York Fed President John Williams said on November 17 that conditions did not call for a dramatic half-point move. The fight is over size and sequence, not direction.

Markets have already voted, and the vote needs handling with care because it changes by the hour and by the venue that measures it. Across futures markets and prediction markets on November 18 and 19, the chance of a quarter-point increase on December 9 sat between roughly 90 and 96 percent, with most of the remainder on a half point, and essentially nothing on a hold or a cut. A month ago those same markets priced a cut. The reversal, not any single percentage, is the fact.

The rest of the market snapshot, as of the close on Wednesday, November 18, tells a more divided story. The S&P 500, the main American stock index, fell 0.2 percent to 7,324, its fifth straight losing day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.1 percent to 50,198. The Nasdaq rose 0.4 percent to 24,430. Treasury yields, the interest rates the government pays to borrow, barely moved at the long end: the 2-year yield held at 4.80 percent and the 10-year eased to 5.07 percent. The bond market is pricing the hike and doubting the hawks at the same time. Spot gold fell about 3.2 percent on the day to about $3,725 an ounce, because higher real interest rates and a stronger dollar make a metal that pays no interest expensive to hold.

Oil fell too, and the reason is supply, not peace. Brent crude, the world benchmark, settled at $91.95 a barrel on November 18, down 1.3 percent, and West Texas Intermediate, the American benchmark, settled at $83.26, down 3.2 percent. American crude stocks rose 3.4 million barrels in the week ending November 13, to 417.8 million barrels. The International Energy Agency’s November report puts world supply in the last quarter at about 105 million barrels a day, 1.7 million barrels a day above demand.

Against that surplus, the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that normally carries about a fifth of the world’s oil, reads as expensive friction rather than shortage. It is also the waterway the Shenzhen declaration’s second point, stable energy flows, is really about. The data firm Kpler counted tanker crossings near 11 a day in early November against about 50 a day before the Iran war. Other trackers give sharply different counts, and nobody’s Hormuz number is settled. What is settled is the direction of the oil price while all of it continues: down, because the world has more oil than it is burning.

That is the terrain the December decision lands on. A quarter-point increase to 4.00 to 4.25 percent is the base case. It raises the cost of every government borrowing to fund Ukraine, every data center financed with floating-rate debt, and every Texas project waiting on a bond sale, and it does so while the long end of the bond market quietly bets the tightening will not last.

Chapter Five

Houston

Mayor Whitmire moved first in the window before the new Texas government exists, kept his immigration order in his own hands, and watched the voters put a policy in the charter where nobody can easily reach it.

Houston’s week was about who holds power in the window before the new Texas government exists, and the mayor moved first.

On November 6, Mayor John Whitmire signed an executive order limiting when Houston police contact federal immigration authorities: only when a person is already going to jail on new charges or warrants and also matches a federal database hit for an immigration warrant. He said on the record that he had consulted the incoming statewide officials and that elections matter. In April he had taken the opposite position after Governor Greg Abbott threatened more than $110 million in public safety funding. The order is the first exercised leverage of the new alignment, and Whitmire knows its limits, because he spent this week defending them.

The outgoing administration is using the courts while it still can. On November 13, Attorney General Ken Paxton’s office asked a Fort Bend County court to block the order, arguing it violates Senate Bill 4, the 2017 law that bars local governments from limiting immigration enforcement. Paxton lost his race for the United States Senate and leaves the attorney general’s office in January, when Democrat Nathan Johnson takes over. The lawsuit’s practical life is therefore measured in weeks, unless a court moves faster than the inauguration.

Whitmire then blocked his own council from making his policy stronger. Three council members, Alejandra Salinas, Edward Pollard and Tiffany Thomas, proposed an ordinance copying the executive order in the mayor’s own language into city law. On November 17, City Attorney Arturo Michel, who reports to the mayor, ruled the ordinance unlawful, which stops a council vote. Whitmire keeps the policy as an act he controls and can defend, rather than a statute that hands the council ownership and hands Paxton a cleaner target. The lever and the liability both stay in the mayor’s office.

The voters, meanwhile, put a policy into the charter where neither the mayor nor the council can easily reach it. Proposition A, approved on November 3, is now part of the city charter: misdemeanor marijuana possession becomes the police department’s lowest enforcement priority, and no-knock warrants are banned. More than 70 percent of voters backed it. Possession remains a state offense. What changed is the order in which Houston police are told to care, and charter language is harder to reverse than an ordinance. A charter amendment is the one decision in this chapter that no incoming officeholder and no court calendar can undo quickly, which is why the voters, not the mayor, now own it.

Harris County’s fight is over flood money and time. On November 12, the Flood Control District told Commissioners Court that $320 million in federal disaster and mitigation grants, administered through the Texas General Land Office, remains at risk against spending deadlines. The composition matters more than the headline: about $80 million of the $113 million disaster portion is excess contingency, money set aside because construction bids came in below the approved amounts, not projects canceled. A one-year extension would cut the at-risk loss to $48 million, and two years would cut it to zero, according to the district’s presentation. The county has created a working group that reports back on February 11, 2027, three weeks after the state government changes hands. The ask will be made to different officeholders than the ones who let the deadlines slip.

The Port of Houston is not waiting for any of them. On November 10 the Port Commission approved a $569 million operating budget and a $397 million capital plan for fiscal 2027, projecting container volumes up 2.5 percent to about 4.6 million standard shipping containers and operating revenue up nearly 5 percent to $763.5 million. Those are projections in an approved budget, not results.

The latest results are September’s: about 376,000 containers, up 11 percent on September 2025, and about 3.35 million through the first nine months, up 2 percent. Customs data for October, which counts imports only, shows Houston adding more import containers than any other top-ten American port that month, up 26.7 percent on September, though the data provider itself cautioned that part of the jump is recovery from a weak September. The port’s capital plan also includes feasibility work on Project 12, the next channel deepening. Its next commission meeting is December 8, the day before the Fed decides. The port prices, builds and dredges on its own calendar regardless of who holds Austin, which is precisely its form of power.

Chapter Six

Texas Permits Before the Audit

Texas resumed issuing data center permits before the grid audit that was supposed to gate them has reported. The audit lands December 10. Permits banked now are facts the next administration inherits.

The cleanest power move in Texas this week was a restart nobody announced with a speech.

In September, Governor Abbott directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality, the state’s environmental regulator, to halt permits for data center projects until the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, the grid operator for most of Texas, finished an audit of the industry. On November 13, the governor’s office notified the regulator that ERCOT had finished gathering community-impact information. Permit reviews resumed. On November 16 the agency issued an air permit for a data center and its gas plant. Industry reporting counts three data center gas plant permits issued that day, and a monitoring group found that 17 construction approvals suspended under the pause were active again by November 13.

The audit itself is not finished. ERCOT files its two reports on December 10: one verifying which large loads, meaning single sites drawing 75 megawatts or more, remain eligible for its one-time group study of grid connections, and one summarizing community impact. The Public Utility Commission, which oversees ERCOT, takes them up at an open meeting expected on December 17. Separately, ERCOT’s pause on switching on new large data centers remains in place until the verification is complete. So the state is now issuing environmental permits for projects it will not yet allow to plug in, under an audit that has not reported, ordered by a governor who leaves office on January 19. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has pledged her own moratorium on data center approvals until the Legislature passes new protections. Every developer in Texas can read that calendar. Permits banked in the next two months are permits the next administration inherits as facts.

The queue those permits feed is mostly paper. About 474 gigawatts of connection requests sit in ERCOT’s queue, roughly 90 percent of them data centers, against a record peak demand of about 91 gigawatts set on July 22. A gigawatt is 1,000 megawatts, enough at peak for roughly 200,000 Texas homes by the usual rule of thumb, though data centers draw steadily rather than at peak. ERCOT’s provisional sorting, called Batch Zero, put 204 projects with 66.4 gigawatts in its base class and 158 projects with 127.9 gigawatts in a studied class, with the rest excluded or unresolved. Seventeen loads totaling about 6,600 megawatts have cleared every other gate and are waiting only for permission to switch on. That last number, not the 474, is the load that is real this winter.

Into that gap stepped ERCOT’s chief executive. On November 11, at a BloombergNEF summit in Houston, Pablo Vegas said he will ask the Legislature to let ERCOT order data centers to cut power at the first stage of a grid emergency, or even before it, rather than waiting for the second stage as current rules require. The alerts are ERCOT’s Energy Emergency Alerts, three stages as spare power runs thin: the first is a warning, and the second is the stage at which ERCOT can order large users to cut. Senate Bill 6, passed in 2025, already requires the largest users to be able to cut consumption with 24 hours’ notice, and no data center has ever been ordered to cut under it. Vegas is asking for a faster trigger, and only the Legislature can give it to him. The Legislature he is asking is not the one that passed Senate Bill 6.

That legislature convenes on January 12, 2027, a week before Hinojosa takes the oath on January 19. Democrats hold the House 83 to 67, their first majority in more than two decades, and Republicans hold the Senate 19 to 12. Representative Senfronia Thompson of Houston, in the House since 1973, says she has 90 pledges for Speaker; 76 votes elect. In the Senate, the presiding officer changes too: Lieutenant Governor-elect Vikki Goodwin, a Democrat, will run a Republican chamber. The rules of the Senate are adopted by the senators themselves, which is the counterweight: a presiding officer’s powers in Texas are largely powers the majority lends her.

Bill filing for the session opened November 9, and data center bills are already arriving from both parties: repealing the industry’s sales tax exemption, requiring water-use disclosure, barring local tax incentives. The fights that decide Texas power in 2027 are therefore already scheduled. December 10 for the audit, December 17 for the commission, January 12 for the legislature, January 19 for the governor. Shenzhen produced four points and no dates. Texas produced no communiqué at all, and everything is dated.

Chapter Seven

Two Rival Reads

Was Shenzhen the founding meeting of a three-power directorate, or theatre while the dated decisions govern? Two coherent answers, and the evidence that separates them.

Read One: the cartel is forming. On this read, Shenzhen was not empty. It was a claim, made in public by the three permanent Security Council members who hold nuclear arsenals, to set the rules themselves: reform the institution that gives them vetoes, manage the world’s refined fuel supply, declare sitting leaders beyond the reach of international courts, and reopen nuclear talks as a three-man club that excludes the other two nuclear powers. The breakthrough was the meeting, the first of its kind, with Putin rehabilitated in the photograph and Xi confirmed as the host the other two must visit. Berlin, on this read, is the reactive performance: louder, larger, and unsigned. What would prove this read: a follow-up trilateral meeting or working group announced within weeks, a dated nuclear dialogue with named participants, or a joint step on oil supply or UN reform that carries a number. Any one of those turns a photograph into a directorate.

Read Two: the texts are theatre and the calendars are the government. On this read, Shenzhen was theatre and Berlin approved nothing, and both rooms know it. The decisions that bind are the ones with dates and majorities attached: a European summit that must find Ukraine’s 2027 money, a Federal Reserve vote, a Texas audit, a legislature. Power this month belongs to whoever controls those rooms, and none of them is a summit. What would prove this read: silence from Shenzhen for 30 days, no working groups and no dates, while the dated decisions land one by one and move money, rates and permits. What would kill it is the same evidence that proves Read One. The two reads cannot both survive a follow-up meeting with an agenda.

Chapter Eight

Scenarios

Three ways the board moves from here, each with the evidence that would confirm it and the evidence that would kill it.

Scenario 1: The dated decisions govern. The European summit approves a version of the 45 billion euro loan, the Fed raises a quarter point and signals January, ERCOT’s December 10 reports clear a modest set of loads, and Shenzhen produces nothing further. Confirm: a Council decision on the loan before the end of November, a 25 basis point move on December 9 with a hawkish statement, Batch Zero classifications close to the provisional ones. Kill: any announced trilateral follow-up with dates and an agenda, which would move the center of gravity back to the summit track.

Scenario 2: The cartel gets a second meeting. A follow-up trilateral or a standing nuclear dialogue is announced, with Russia treating it as the main channel and Europe’s role shrinking to funder. Confirm: a named dialogue with a date, a joint oil-supply step with volumes, or American language adopting the three-power format for Ukraine. Kill: 30 days of silence from all three capitals on any follow-up, or a Berlin guarantee text signed with named troop contributors and an American backstop in writing.

Scenario 3: The Fed breaks the script. December brings a half-point increase, or a quarter point with an explicit January signal that reprices the whole path. Confirm: November jobs on December 4 printing strong with unemployment at or below 4.1 percent, October PCE on November 25 at or above September’s 3.1 percent core reading, or Waller’s position appearing in the statement’s language. Kill: a weak December 4 jobs report with unemployment above 4.3 percent, or core PCE falling back toward 3.0 percent, either of which hands the gradualists the argument.

Chapter Nine

Watchlist

Five developments that would change the analysis.

November 25: October PCE and the second estimate of third-quarter growth. Core PCE at or above 3.1 percent keeps the half-point argument alive into December. A fall toward 3.0 percent takes it off the table.

November 26 and 27: the extraordinary European summit on Ukraine financing. Approval of the 45 billion euro loan, in any form, converts Berlin’s veto into funding. Another deferral leaves Ukraine’s 2027 gap open and raises the value of the frozen assets Europe has not touched.

December 4 and December 9: November jobs, then the Fed. Jobs decide the size of the move; the statement decides whether December is one increase or the start of a sequence. Watch the vote split as much as the rate.

December 10 and December 17: ERCOT’s audit reports, then the Public Utility Commission. Which loads survive verification, and whether permits issued in November stand, will show whether the restart was a head start or a fait accompli.

Any trilateral follow-up within 30 days. A date, a working group or an agenda from Shenzhen would prove Read One and demote every other item on this list. Silence proves Read Two by default.
